title: Phase 6: Automated unit and integration tests
description: Build a layered test suite using xUnit and Moq for domain and handler unit tests, Respawn + WebApplicationFactory for integration tests, and React Testing Library for frontend component tests. Target 80%+ line coverage on domain and application layers.

data.text: Tests are the only safety net you have when refactoring legacy code or upgrading dependencies. In a senior-level project, tests are not an afterthought — they define the observable behavior of the system. This phase establishes the test pyramid: fast unit tests at the base, slower integration tests in the middle, and a handful of critical-path E2E tests at the top.

data.caption: Test pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, fewest E2E tests

graph BT E2E[E2E Tests
Playwright, slow, flaky] --> INT[Integration Tests
WebApplicationFactory, moderate] INT --> UNIT[Unit Tests
xUnit + Moq, fast, reliable] style E2E fill:#f9f,stroke:#333 style INT fill:#bbf,stroke:#333 style UNIT fill:#9f9,stroke:#333

data.text: Domain tests have zero infrastructure dependencies. They prove that aggregate invariants hold under all legal and illegal state transitions.

data.title: C#: ExpenseReport aggregate unit tests
data.content: Use xUnit theory tests for combinatorial inputs and FluentAssertions for readable assertions.

data.text: Mock repository and policy engine interfaces. Verify that handlers call the right domain methods and persist changes via the unit of work.

data.title: C#: SubmitExpenseReportHandler unit test
data.content: Moq creates a fake repository without touching a database.

data.text: WebApplicationFactory spins up the real API in-memory. Respawn resets the database to a clean checkpoint between tests, keeping tests isolated without dropping and recreating the schema each time.

data.title: C#: Integration test fixture with Respawn checkpoint
data.content: Fixture creates the API host and provides a clean database for each test.

data.text: React Testing Library tests assert behavior from the user's perspective: does the button fire a submit call? Does the error banner appear on failure?

data.title: TypeScript: NewExpenseReportForm test
data.content: Mock the API mutation and assert UI state transitions.

data.title: Use collection fixtures for shared infrastructure
data.text: xUnit Collection fixtures ensure WebApplicationFactory is created once per test class, not once per test method. This keeps integration tests fast enough to run in CI.

items.text: Domain unit tests cover all aggregate invariants (submit, approve, reject, add line item, duplicate detection).
Handler unit tests use Moq to verify repository and policy interactions.
Integration tests prove POST /api/expense-reports returns 201 with the correct shape.
Respawn checkpoint resets the database between tests without dropping schema.
React Testing Library tests cover form submission, error display, and loading states.
CI pipeline runs dotnet test and npm test on every PR.

data.title: Phase 6 summary
points: Domain tests are fast and require no infrastructure — cover them first.
Integration tests prove the full stack works together (EF Core → SQL Server → HTTP → JSON).
React Testing Library tests assert user-visible behavior, not implementation details.
CI gate: no PR merges without passing tests.
data.takeaway: Tests are living documentation. If a new developer can understand the domain by reading the test names, you've written them well.
